questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Definite Integral of Function Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =5x-6 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =5 \\ \text{d}u & =5\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{5}\text{d}u & =\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=5x-6.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 2 & 3 \\ u & 4 & 9\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}\sqrt{{(5x-6)}^{3}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{4}^{9}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{9}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{4}^{9}{u}^{3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot {\frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}|}_{4}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{2}{5}({9}^{5/2}-{4}^{5/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{25}(({3}^{2})^{5/2}-({2}^{2})^{5/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{25}({3}^{5}-{2}^{5}) \\  & =\frac{2}{25}(243-32) \\  & =\frac{422}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality Involving Two Logarithmic Functions
questions.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $10.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(2-x)+1} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+9)} \\ {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(2-x)}\cdot {10}^{1} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+9)} \\ (2-x)\cdot 10 & \le x+9 \\ 20-10x & \le x+9 \\ -11x & \le -11 \\ x & \ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & <2 \\ x+9 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-9\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\ge 1,$ which can be expressed as $[1,\infty ).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x<2$ and $x>-11,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,2)$ and $(-11,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
[1,\infty )\cap (-\infty ,2)\cap (-9,\infty )=[1,2)
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in [1,2),$ which can also be written as $1\le x<2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Complex Number in Exponential Form
questions.problem: Write the complex number $z=3-\text{i}\sqrt{3}$ in exponential form.
questions.worked_solution:
To write our complex number in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{(-\sqrt{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant, we can find the angle $\theta $ as

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =2\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})| \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{11\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=2\sqrt{3}$ and $\theta =\frac{11\pi }{6}$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get

$$
z=2\sqrt{3}\,{\text{e}}^{11\pi \text{i}/6}.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Writing a Complex Number in Exponential Form

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Cubic Polynomial Given One Real Root, Two Complex Roots, and a Leading Coefficient
questions.problem:
The cubic polynomial $f(x)$ has roots ${x}_{1}=5,{x}_{2,3}=-1\pm 2\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the cubic term is $-4.$ Find $f(x).$

$f(x)=$
{{field-1}}${x}^{3}\,+$
{{field-2}}${x}^{2}\,+$
{{field-3}}$x\,+$
{{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
Since $f(x)$ has roots ${x}_{1}=5$ and ${x}_{2,3}=-1\pm 2\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the cubic term is $a=-4,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2})(x-{x}_{3}) \\  & =-4(x-5)(x-(-1+2\text{i}))(x-(-1-2\text{i})) \\  & =-4(x-5)(x-(-1+2\text{i}))(x-(-1-2\text{i}))\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-4(x-5)(x-(-1+2\text{i}))(x-(-1-2\text{i})) & = \\ -4(x-5)({x}^{2}-x(-1-2\text{i})-x(-1+2\text{i})+(-1+2\text{i})(-1-2\text{i})) & = \\ -4(x-5)({x}^{2}+2x+5) & = \\ -4({x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}+5x-5{x}^{2}-10x-25) & = \\ -4({x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-5x-25) & = \\ -4{x}^{3}+12{x}^{2}+20x+100.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)=-4{x}^{3}+12{x}^{2}+20x+100.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Magnitude of a Vector-Valued Function
questions.worked_solution:
Evaluating the function at $t=6,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(6) & =⟨\sqrt{6+1},\,6-3⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{7},\,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the magnitude of this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|r(6)| & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{7})}^{2}+{(3)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{7+9} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Intervals on Which a Given Function Satisfies the Extreme Value Theorem
questions.problem:
On which of the following intervals can the extreme value theorem be applied to the function $y={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)}?$ 

- $(-2,2]$
- $[-2,4]$
- $(-2,4)$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the extreme value theorem is only applicable to closed intervals on which the function is continuous.

With that in mind, let's take a look at each interval.

- The interval $(-2,2]$ is not closed, so the extreme value theorem is not applicable.

- The interval $[-2,4]$ is closed, and the function is continuous on $[-2,4].$ Therefore, the extreme value theorem is applicable.

- The interval $(-2,4)$ is not closed, so the extreme value theorem is not applicable.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "II only".

provenance.kp_title: Identifying Intervals on Which a Given Function Satisfies the Extreme Value Theorem
